title: Graph Algorithms
description: Breadth-first and depth-first search, shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, topological sorting and flows, with their uses in machine learning.
overview: Graphs model relationships, so graph algorithms answer the basic questions about them: what can be reached from here, what is the shortest route, how can everything be connected most cheaply, in what order must tasks run, how much can flow through a network. The same handful of algorithms also appears inside machine learning, from the order in which a neural network's computation is evaluated to the importance ranking of web pages and the clusters found in a data set.

This chapter develops traversal (BFS and DFS), shortest paths (Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford), spanning trees (Kruskal, Prim), topological order and a first look at flows and matching. It builds on the graph definitions of Discrete Mathematics and the queues, heaps and hash tables of Data Structures.
objectives: Implement BFS and DFS, and use them for shortest paths in unweighted graphs, connected components and cycle detection.
Run Dijkstra's algorithm by hand, state its complexity and limitations, and know when to use Bellman–Ford.
Compute a minimum spanning tree with Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms and explain the cut property.
Produce a topological order of a DAG and explain its role in computational graphs.
Describe maximum flow, bipartite matching and PageRank, and identify graph algorithms in machine learning.

sections.title: Graph traversal: BFS and DFS
body: A graph is stored as an adjacency list (a dictionary from each vertex to the list of its neighbors) so that scanning the neighbors of a vertex costs its degree. A **traversal** visits every vertex reachable from a start vertex, each exactly once, using a **visited** set to avoid looping on cycles. Total cost: O(V + E), since each vertex is processed once and each edge examined once (twice in an undirected graph).

**BFS** explores in layers: first the start, then its neighbors, then their neighbors. It uses a **queue**. Because it reaches vertices in order of increasing distance, BFS finds **shortest paths in unweighted graphs**, measured in number of edges.

code: """graph: dict mapping vertex -> list of neighbors. Returns hop counts from start."""
if v not in dist:             # first time we reach v: shortest
body.caption: BFS computes the number of edges on a shortest path from the start.

body: **DFS** goes as deep as possible along one path before backtracking. It uses a **stack**, usually the call stack of a recursive function.

body.caption: DFS visits everything reachable from u. Running it from each unvisited vertex finds the connected components.

list: **Connected components**: the groups of mutually reachable vertices (for example, the clusters that result from linking all pairs of data points within distance ε).
**Cycle detection**: in a directed graph, DFS finds a cycle exactly when it meets a vertex that is still on the current recursion path.
**Topological order** and strongly connected components are built from DFS finishing times.

**Search in state spaces**: puzzles, game trees and planning problems are graphs whose vertices are states. BFS finds the fewest moves; DFS uses little memory and explores deep solutions; iterative deepening combines both.

sections.title: Shortest paths
body: In a graph with edge weights (distances, costs, travel times), the length of a path is the sum of its edge weights. **Dijkstra's algorithm** finds the shortest paths from one source to all vertices when all weights are non-negative. It is greedy: repeatedly settle the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance, since no other route can reach it more cheaply, and then **relax** its outgoing edges (replace dist[v] by dist[u] + w(u, v) if that is smaller).

code: """graph: dict u -> list of (v, weight). Returns shortest distances from source."""
heap = [(0, source)]                    # priority queue of (distance, vertex)
if d > dist.get(u, float('inf')):   # stale entry: skip
body.caption: Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary heap: O((V + E) log V).

example.title: Dijkstra by hand
example.problem: Undirected edges: A–B 4, A–C 2, B–C 1, B–D 5, C–D 8, C–E 10, D–E 2, D–F 6, E–F 3. Find the shortest distances from A.
solution: The distances are A 0, B 3, C 2, D 8, E 10, F 13. The shortest path to F is A → C → B → D → E → F (2 + 1 + 5 + 2 + 3 = 13). The direct-looking route A–B has length 4, but going through C is shorter, 3.

list: Dijkstra needs **non-negative** weights. With a negative edge, a settled vertex's distance can later improve, and the greedy step fails.
**Bellman–Ford** relaxes all edges V − 1 times: O(VE). It handles negative weights and detects negative cycles (a cycle whose weights sum to less than zero, which makes shortest paths undefined).
**Floyd–Warshall** computes all pairs of distances by dynamic programming in O(V³): d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]) over intermediate vertices k.

**A\* search** speeds up Dijkstra toward a single target by ordering vertices by distance so far plus a heuristic estimate of the remaining distance. It is optimal if the heuristic never overestimates, and it is the standard for route planning and game AI.

sections.title: Minimum spanning trees
body: A **spanning tree** of a connected graph is a tree that includes all the vertices (V − 1 edges). A **minimum spanning tree** (MST) is the spanning tree of least total edge weight: the cheapest way to connect everything (cabling a network, for instance).

body.key: Cut property: for any partition of the vertices into two groups, the lightest edge crossing between the groups belongs to some MST. Every greedy MST algorithm is an application of this fact.

list: **Kruskal's algorithm**: sort the edges by weight; go through them in order and add an edge if it does not form a cycle with the edges already chosen. Cycle checks use **union–find**, which maintains the connected groups with near-constant cost per operation. Total O(E log E), dominated by the sort.
**Prim's algorithm**: grow a tree from one vertex, always adding the cheapest edge leading out of the tree, found with a priority queue. O(E log V).

example.title: Kruskal's algorithm
example.problem: Find an MST of the graph used in the Dijkstra example.
example.solution: Sorted edges: B–C 1, D–E 2, A–C 2, E–F 3, A–B 4, B–D 5, D–F 6, C–D 8, C–E 10. Take B–C (1), D–E (2), A–C (2), E–F (3). A–B would connect A and B, which are already joined through C: skip. B–D (5) joins the groups {A, B, C} and {D, E, F}: take. That makes 5 = V − 1 edges, so we stop. Total weight 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 5 = 13.

body: An MST is not the same as a tree of shortest paths: in the example, the shortest path from A to F uses the edge C–B–D–E–F, but the MST connects things by a different criterion (total weight). In machine learning, **single-linkage clustering** is exactly Kruskal's algorithm: process the edges between data points in order of distance and merge groups; cutting the longest MST edges gives the clusters (see Clustering). MSTs also give approximation algorithms for the travelling salesman problem and appear in Chow–Liu trees for graphical models.

sections.title: Topological sorting and DAGs
body: A **topological order** of a directed acyclic graph lists the vertices so that every edge u → v has u before v. It exists exactly when there is no directed cycle, and it is the order in which dependent tasks can be carried out: compile a library after the libraries it needs, run a course after its prerequisites, evaluate a node of a computation after its inputs.

**Kahn's algorithm**: compute each vertex's in-degree. Repeatedly remove a vertex of in-degree zero, output it, and decrease the in-degree of its successors. If vertices remain at the end, there is a cycle. Time O(V + E). (A DFS that outputs vertices in reverse finishing order also works.)

code: """graph: dict u -> list of successors. Returns an order, or None if cyclic."""
ready = deque(u for u in graph if indeg[u] == 0)
return order if len(order) == len(graph) else None
body.caption: Kahn's algorithm.

list: **Neural networks**: the forward pass evaluates the computational graph in topological order, and backpropagation visits it in the reverse order (see Automatic Differentiation).
**Build systems and pipelines** (make, data-processing workflows) schedule steps in topological order, running independent steps in parallel.

**Longest path in a DAG** (the critical path that determines the minimum completion time of a project) is solved by dynamic programming in topological order in O(V + E), while it is NP-hard on general graphs.

sections.title: Flows, matching and graphs in machine learning
body: In a **flow network** each edge has a capacity, and we want to send as much as possible from a source to a sink. The **max-flow min-cut theorem** states that the maximum flow equals the capacity of the smallest set of edges whose removal disconnects the sink from the source (the minimum cut). The Ford–Fulkerson method repeatedly finds a path with spare capacity and pushes flow along it. Max-flow solves scheduling, routing and image segmentation (a minimum cut separates foreground from background pixels).

A **matching** pairs up vertices of a bipartite graph (workers and jobs, predictions and ground-truth objects). Maximum matching reduces to max-flow. The **assignment problem**, a matching of minimum total cost, is solved by the **Hungarian algorithm** in O(n³). It is used to assign predicted boxes to labeled objects when training object detectors, to align clusters with classes when evaluating clustering, and, with the cost being a distance between distributions, in optimal transport.

body.h: Where graphs appear in machine learning

list: **PageRank**: the importance of a web page is the stationary distribution of a random surfer who follows links with probability 0.85 and jumps to a random page otherwise. It is the dominant eigenvector of the 'Google matrix' and is computed by power iteration, each step a sparse matrix–vector product, a pass over the edges (see Eigenvalues).

**Graph neural networks** update each vertex's feature vector by aggregating its neighbors' vectors, h_v ← σ(W · mean of h_u over neighbors u). They learn on molecules, social networks and knowledge graphs.
**Spectral clustering and semi-supervised label propagation** use the graph Laplacian of a similarity graph over the data (see Clustering).
**Manifold learning**: Isomap approximates distances along a curved data surface by shortest paths in a k-nearest-neighbor graph.
**Recommendation**: users and items form a bipartite graph; collaborative filtering uses paths and random walks on it.

**Probabilistic graphical models** use trees, junction trees and message passing on graphs (see Graphical Models); the Chow–Liu algorithm builds the best tree-structured model as a maximum spanning tree of pairwise mutual information.
**Computational graphs** are DAGs, handled by topological ordering.

example.title: A PageRank step
example.problem: Three pages: 1 links to 2 and 3; 2 links to 3; 3 links to 1. With damping d = 0.85, starting from the uniform vector (1/3, 1/3, 1/3), compute one update of PageRank.
example.solution: The new rank of page j is (1 − d)/3 + d Σ_{i → j} r_i/outdegree(i), with (1 − d)/3 = 0.05. Page 1 receives from page 3 (outdegree 1): 0.05 + 0.85(1/3) = 0.333. Page 2 receives from page 1 (outdegree 2): 0.05 + 0.85(1/6) = 0.192. Page 3 receives from page 1 (half of its rank) and page 2 (all of it): 0.05 + 0.85(1/6 + 1/3) = 0.475. They sum to 1.0. Page 3, which is linked to by both others, ranks highest.

summary: BFS (queue) and DFS (stack) traverse a graph in O(V + E). BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS finds components, cycles and topological orders.

Dijkstra's algorithm settles vertices in order of tentative distance, O((V + E) log V) with a heap, for non-negative weights. Bellman–Ford handles negative weights in O(VE), Floyd–Warshall computes all pairs in O(V³), A* adds a heuristic.

A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices with least total weight; Kruskal (sort and union–find) and Prim (heap) are greedy and rest on the cut property. Single-linkage clustering is Kruskal's algorithm.
A topological order of a DAG (Kahn's algorithm, O(V + E)) respects dependencies; neural networks are evaluated forward in topological order and differentiated in reverse.
Max flow equals min cut; the Hungarian algorithm solves assignment. Graph algorithms appear in PageRank, graph neural networks, spectral methods, Isomap and recommendation.

problems.q: Run BFS from vertex 1 on the graph 1–2, 1–3, 2–4, 3–4, 4–5 and give the distances and one shortest path to 5.
problems.solution: Distances: 1: 0; 2 and 3: 1; 4: 2; 5: 3. A shortest path to 5 is 1 → 2 → 4 → 5.

problems.q: Directed graph with edges S→A (7), S→B (2), B→A (3), A→T (1), B→T (8). Use Dijkstra to find the shortest distance from S to T and the path.
problems.solution: Start: S 0. Settle S: A = 7, B = 2. Settle B (2): A = min(7, 2 + 3) = 5, T = 2 + 8 = 10. Settle A (5): T = min(10, 5 + 1) = 6. Settle T (6). The shortest distance is 6, via S → B → A → T.

problems.q: Give a topological order of the tasks with prerequisites: shirt before tie, tie before jacket, pants before shoes, pants before belt, belt before jacket.
problems.solution: Edges: shirt→tie, tie→jacket, pants→shoes, pants→belt, belt→jacket. Vertices of in-degree 0: shirt and pants. One order: shirt, pants, tie, belt, shoes, jacket. Another: pants, shoes, belt, shirt, tie, jacket.
problems.a: For example shirt, pants, tie, belt, shoes, jacket.

problems.q: Find an MST of the graph with edges a–b 3, a–c 1, b–c 2, b–d 4, c–d 5 and its weight.
problems.solution: Sorted: a–c 1, b–c 2, a–b 3, b–d 4, c–d 5. Take a–c, b–c; a–b would form a cycle (a–c–b), skip; take b–d. Total 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 with 3 edges for 4 vertices.

problems.q: Why can Dijkstra's algorithm fail with a negative edge? Give a small example.
problems.solution: Take S→A (2), S→B (3), B→A (−2). Dijkstra settles A first with distance 2 (the smallest tentative distance), but the path S→B→A has length 1. After settling A, the algorithm never revisits it, so it reports 2 instead of 1.
problems.a: A settled vertex may later get a shorter route through a negative edge; Dijkstra reports 2 where the true distance is 1.
